name: Carlos Rahman

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I’m a senior researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent group. We have no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, political parties or government; we sell nothing and campaign for no side. Your answers are confidential. What does your usual shift involve?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I’m 58 and take late calls and chats about missed trains and ticket changes at a contact centre. I finished secondary school and have handled these fares for years, at about the same pace as other experienced agents; I do not run the desk. The night cover rate lifts my pay above the usual agent wage. I use the approved AI journey summary now and then after another agent has checked a route, but I open the actual ticket record before offering a seat.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What has that wage done for your household?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: My partner Leila checks stock at a pharmacy, and our grown children live in their own homes. We rent and have ten months of expenses saved; plenty of contact centres are nearby, but few offer this night rate. We would like more evenings together eventually, though we have not established income to replace my shift pay. I like getting a stranded traveller onto a real departure, even if it takes an extra call.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would say a quicker route summary helps when a customer is stranded. I would still open the ticket record and check that the replacement seat actually exists.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I expect my late calls and Leila’s pharmacy shifts to carry on. Ten months saved gives us room for an ordinary repair, but I would not use it to buy time off without a wage plan.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In 2026 I will keep taking missed-train calls and checking the ticket before I promise another departure. In the first year of small change, I will put thirty from each paid night-cover week into the car-repair envelope while that premium continues.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel calm about the work and grateful for the night rate. A tidy route map cannot put a stranded traveller on the right platform.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: When did a route summary get it wrong?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Last week the summary suggested a connection that had already left before the first train arrived. I checked the actual timetable and found a later seat that the customer could use.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What is the reserve for?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Leila and I would use the ten-month reserve for a genuine gap or repair. Our grown children have their own costs, and their wages are not part of our retirement calculation.

say: I would check **actual seats** before promising a new departure.
I would use **route summaries** as help, not as a ticket record.
think: I expect my **late calls** and Leila’s shifts to continue.
I keep **ten months saved** for real repair or wage gaps.
do: Keep taking **missed-train calls** and checking ticket records in 2026.
Save **thirty weekly** for car repairs only while the paid night premium continues.
feel: **Calm** about the night wage and ordinary work.

steps.text: Keep answering missed-train calls and checking original ticket records
Save thirty from each paid night-cover week for car repairs while premium lasts

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell the late desk that software will take easy fare changes before it handles a stranded family well. I would ask to see paid night hours beside the new rebooking total.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The night premium could disappear before the job does. My ten-month reserve gives us choice, but a daytime post nearby may still pay much less for a full week.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In 2026 I will test the new AI rebooking assistant on eighteen closed missed-connection cases during a paid shift if my supervisor lets me record false offers. When routine calls move in the first year, I will keep paid night calls and compare three posted paid station-desk jobs by written weekly wages and hours after travel. If my night hours fall, I will apply only where those terms cover rent and utilities and the last bus gets me home; I will stay on this job until a suitable offer is signed.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I am anxious about losing the premium, though I can test a tool that colleagues have checked. A late train still needs a person who can find a real seat.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you count in the AI test?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would count false connections and seats that vanish when the customer clicks. A faster answer is no help if it sends someone to an empty platform.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why does the bus matter?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A station counter might close after the last bus from that side of town. I will look at the end of a paid week as well as its wage before applying.

say: I would ask for **paid night hours** beside software rebooking totals.
I would count **false connections** when the new assistant is tested.
think: I may lose the **night premium** before the whole job.
I know **daytime wages** may be lower despite ten months saved.
do: Test the **new AI rebooking assistant** on eighteen closed cases during paid time if false offers can be logged.
Keep **paid night calls** and compare three posted station jobs by written weekly wages/hours after travel.
Apply if **night hours fall** only for posted paid work covering rent/utilities after travel with last-bus access; stay until signed.
feel: **Anxious** about night pay, willing to test proven software.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell coworkers full thinking AI by 2028 could rebook most missed trains without my headset. Physical robots around 2031 come later, but the fare-changing work is already on a screen.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think night calls could end before a station desk has room for me. Ten months saved and many nearby centres make a careful search possible, yet Leila and I still need a weekly wage.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In 2026 I will compare posted paid station information-desk hours with the last eight night pay slips. If my calls end in the first year after 2028, Leila and I will cap the search at four weeks of existing savings while I apply for posted paid work that has written weekly wages and hours covering rent and utilities after travel and a last bus home; I will leave the paid night rota only after a suitable signed offer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I am anxious about a quick wage gap, but we have room to reject a weak rota. Ten months saved buys a careful search, not a wage that repeats every Friday.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would a station desk actually do?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would ask whether the station desk can reissue a missed ticket or only point to a screen. A paid post with no power to solve a traveller’s problem may not last long.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would you limit the search?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We would agree on the four-week search cap before touching the reserve. Our children cannot be asked to replace the night premium just because we have saved some money.

say: I would separate **2028 screen work** from physical robots arriving around 2031.
I would compare **posted station hours** with my real night pay slips.
think: I see **night calls** at risk before another desk opens.
I know **ten months saved** allows a search, not a lasting wage.
do: Compare **eight night pay slips** with posted paid station-desk hours and ask about ticket-reissue duties.
Use at most **four weeks** of existing savings for search only if calls end after 2028.
Apply after calls end for **posted paid local work** with written rent/utility-covering weekly wages/hours after travel, last bus; leave when signed.
feel: **Anxious** about quick night-pay loss, with room to choose.
S2.quote: Ten months saved buys a careful search, not a wage that repeats every Friday.
fieldNote: The **four-week cap** uses existing savings and is not a new saving action.
He **asks about reissue power** because a powerless counter may be short-lived.
The signed move needs **written weekly terms** and a last bus home.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would say five years lets us inspect an actual station counter rather than imagine a safe job there. Thinking AGI reaches the phone desk by 2031, and robots for physical station work arrive around 2034.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I might keep night callers with complicated journeys for longer, but a premium can shrink without a dismissal letter. Ten months saved means I can inspect a trial without making Leila’s wage our whole plan.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: From 2026 I will keep paid disruption calls and ask for a single paid station-counter shadow afternoon only if the manager can cover my night hours and show a posted opening. If that counter can reissue tickets and its written weekly wages and hours cover rent and utilities after travel, I will apply when my call hours fall in the first year after 2031; I will not leave the night job before a suitable offer is signed.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel anxious about losing paid nights, though the longer warning gives me time to look. A shadow afternoon is evidence of a job, not its weekly wage.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What authority would you need at the counter?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would ask who can change a ticket after the train has departed. If a counter agent only passes a note upstairs, I would not switch for a new badge.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would Leila compare?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Leila and I would put the posted week beside the rent, utilities and last bus. We would keep the reserve for a real gap rather than spend it on an unposted promise.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would say a decade is time to measure what a shorter night week would actually pay. Thinking AGI reaches rebooking by 2036, with robots for hands-on station work around 2039.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At 68 I might want to stop nights, but Leila and I have not worked out reliable income to replace the premium. Ten months saved is a buffer against gaps, not a date for leaving work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In 2026 I will keep the paid night rota and review our rent, utilities, wages and any verified later-life income with Leila each year. If I still need a wage after 2036 and night calls fall, I will compare posted paid daytime station and centre work by written weekly wages and hours after travel, with a last bus home; I will move only on a suitable signed offer that covers the bills.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel uneasy about the far end and reasonably steady now. I cannot put a departure time on retirement until I know what arrives in the account.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would let you leave nights?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would ask for an actual income figure and an actual paid rota before cutting nights. A hope that the reserve will last is not a monthly payment.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would the children join the budget?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Our grown children have their own homes to fund. We can tell them what we decide, but we will not add their pay to our sheet.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 worries me most because a machine could rebook a journey before the night team has time to find other paid work. Ten months saved and many nearby centres give us a search, not a promise of the same wage. I would want written shift dates and a posted station opening whose full weekly pay and hours cover rent and utilities after travel.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: An hourly rate is not a Friday pay packet. I have seen a two-night rota printed beside a generous number that would not cover the rent.

headlineQuote: An hourly rate is not a Friday pay packet.
portrait: Carlos is a **58-year-old experienced agent** with secondary school and above-usual night cover pay.
He uses **AI occasionally**, checking the ticket record before offering a real seat.
Carlos and Leila rent with **ten months saved** and many nearby centres; their grown children live independently.
He compares **whole-week wages** and late transport before any job change, without assuming retirement income.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028** could remove the night rebooking queue before another equally paid week is available.
whatWouldHelp: **Written shift dates** and a posted station job with rent-and-utilities-covering weekly wages and hours after travel would help.
